attribution.credit: Adapted from Tutorial 1 of the LAMMPS Tutorials by Gravelle, Alvares, Gissinger and Kohlmeyer.

concepts.explain: In lj units every quantity is dimensionless: distances are multiples of σ, energies multiples of ε, and masses multiples of the particle mass. Nothing is in angstroms or kcal/mol.
Every atom carries a numeric type. Force field parameters are assigned per type, not per atom, so the type is what selects which parameters apply to a given pair.
A region is a named shape in space and nothing more. The simulation box is built from a region, and only once the box exists can atoms exist.
An integer that fixes the sequence of random numbers. The same seed reproduces a run exactly; changing it gives a statistically independent repeat of the same experiment.
Beyond the cutoff r_{c} the pair interaction is simply not computed. Too short clips the attractive well and the fluid will not condense; too long spends time on forces that are almost zero.
Parameters for unlike pairs are derived from the like pairs rather than written out. LAMMPS uses geometric averages by default; pair_modify selects another rule.
Every fix reads the same way: an ID you choose, the group of atoms it acts on, then the style and that style's own arguments.
The integrator advances time in discrete jumps. Each jump must be short compared with the fastest motion in the system, or the integration stops tracking it and goes unstable.
LAMMPS prints a line of thermodynamic data every so many steps. These are instantaneous values at that step, not running averages, and the GUI charts whichever columns you ask for.
A named subset of the atoms. Groups can be built from types, from regions, or from set operations on other groups, and most commands act on one.
A text file holding the box, the atoms, their types and positions, and the force field parameters. Writing one lets a later run start from this state instead of rebuilding it.
An expression evaluated during the run that returns a single number, so it can be printed alongside the thermo output. Other styles include atom, index, loop, file and vector.
A compute calculates nothing on its own and is not run automatically. Something has to reference it -- another compute, a fix, or a thermo_style column -- before it is evaluated.

steps.title: Choose the rules of the world
steps.teach:
This is your input script, and for now it is only an outline.

A LAMMPS input script is read strictly top to bottom, and the order matters: some commands only work *before* the simulation box exists, others only after, and only a few work in both places. Rather than memorise that, the script is laid out in five labelled sections and filled in turn. Everything after a `#` is a comment, so the headings you see are notes to yourself and nothing more.

Over the next steps each section fills in, one command at a time, and you will end up with a script that runs.
steps.call_to_action: Press Next to write the first line.

steps.title: The unit system
steps.teach:
The first section sets the global choices: the units, the dimensionality, what kind of particle you are simulating, and what happens at the edges of the box.

Strictly speaking none of the four commands in this section is mandatory -- each one matches a LAMMPS default. Writing them down anyway is considered good practice: the next person to read your script should not have to know what the defaults are, and defaults can change between versions.

commands.explain: Work in reduced units, where every quantity is dimensionless. This unit system is the usual choice for simulations exploring general statistical-mechanical behaviour, because it emphasises the relative sizes of the parameters rather than representing any one specific material.

notes.note: the unit system
notes.alternatives: `real` gives angstroms, femtoseconds and kcal/mol; `metal` gives angstroms, picoseconds and eV. Changing this changes the meaning of every number below it, so it comes first.

commands.explain: Run the simulation in three-dimensional space.

notes.note: number of spatial dimensions
notes.alternatives: `2` confines the atoms to move only in the xy-plane. Two-dimensional systems are much cheaper and are often used for visual demonstrations, but they are a different physical system, not a cheaper version of the same one.

commands.explain: Use the simplest kind of particle: a point with a mass and a type, and nothing else. This is the most basic atom style LAMMPS offers.

notes.note: what each atom carries
notes.alternatives: Other styles add attributes: `charge` gives each atom a charge, `molecular` adds bonds, angles and molecule IDs, `sphere` adds a radius and angular velocity. Pick the cheapest style that holds what your model needs.

commands.explain: Apply periodic boundary conditions along all three directions of space. An atom leaving one face of the box re-enters through the opposite one, so a small box behaves like a slice of something much larger.

notes.note: the three letters set x, then y, then z
notes.alternatives: The alternatives are `f` for fixed non-periodic, `s` for shrink-wrapped non-periodic, and `m` for shrink-wrapped with a minimum. Each direction is set independently, so `p p fm` is valid and is the sort of thing a slab geometry uses.

steps.title: A box, and atoms in it
steps.teach:
The next step is to create the simulation box and populate it with atoms.

The system is a binary mixture: 1500 small atoms of type 1 and 100 larger ones of type 2, placed at random.

commands.explain: Define a region named `simbox` that is a block -- a rectangular cuboid -- extending from -20 to 20 units along all three spatial dimensions. A region is only a shape in space; nothing exists in it yet.

notes.note: the name you will refer to it by
the shape
notes.alternatives: `sphere`, `cylinder` and `prism` are also available, and regions can be combined with union and intersect. You will use a cylinder in the second half of this tutorial.

notes.note: the six bounds, as xlo xhi ylo yhi zlo zhi
notes.alternatives: Shrinking the box while keeping the atom count fixed raises the density, which changes the physics rather than just the picture.

commands.explain: Build the actual simulation box from the `simbox` region, reserving space for two types of atom. Every atom in LAMMPS carries an atom type, and that type selects which force field parameters -- here the Lennard-Jones ε_{ij} and σ_{ij} -- apply to each pair, through the pair_coeff command below.

notes.note: how many atom types will ever exist
notes.alternatives: From this point the number of types is locked in: any command referencing a type larger than 2 is an error. You may allocate more types than you need, but every type declared must be given a mass and force field parameters, or LAMMPS stops with an error.

commands.explain: Generate 1500 atoms of type 1 at random positions inside the `simbox` region, then 100 atoms of type 2 the same way. Each atom is automatically given a unique atom ID, numbered from 1 upwards.

notes.note: how many atoms to create
notes.alternatives: More atoms give better statistics and a slower run. 1500 and 100 is small enough to finish on a laptop.

notes.note: the seed for the internal random number generator
notes.alternatives: Changing it produces a different sequence of random numbers and so a different set of initial positions -- a statistically independent repeat of the same experiment.

notes.note: minimum separation enforced while placing atoms
notes.alternatives: Without it, two atoms can be placed almost on top of each other. That produces a close contact, an enormous force from the repulsive branch of the potential, and an unstable simulation. It is the same instability you will meet deliberately later.

commands.explain: The second species, with its own seed so the two sets of positions are independent.

notes.note: the atom type being created

steps.title: Masses
steps.teach: Now the settings for the two atom types. Nothing can be computed until every type has a mass and every pair of types knows how to interact.

commands.explain: Assign a mass of 1.0 to atoms of type 1 and 5.0 to atoms of type 2. In reduced units these are multiples of a reference particle mass, so type 2 is simply five times heavier and will move more sluggishly at the same temperature.

notes.note: which atom type this mass applies to

commands.explain: The heavier species.

steps.title: The Lennard-Jones potential
steps.teach:
The atoms interact through a Lennard-Jones potential, truncated at a cutoff r_{c}:

**E_{ij}(r) = 4ε_{ij} [ (σ_{ij}/r)^{12} − (σ_{ij}/r)^{6} ]**, for r < r_{c}

Here r is the inter-particle distance, ε_{ij} is the depth of the potential well and sets the interaction strength, and σ_{ij} is the distance at which the potential energy crosses zero. The indices i and j refer to a pair of atoms with those atom types.

The r^{−12} term is the steep repulsion that keeps atoms apart at close range; the r^{−6} term is the weaker long-range attraction that lets a fluid condense rather than disperse.

commands.explain: All pairs of atoms interact through the truncated Lennard-Jones potential above, with a cutoff of 4.0 length units.

notes.note: the interaction model
notes.alternatives: `lj/cut/coul/long` adds long-range electrostatics, `eam` is for metals, `airebo` for reactive carbon. This one line decides the physics of the whole simulation.

notes.note: the global cutoff r_{c}, in length units
notes.alternatives: 2.5σ is the more common convention in the published literature; 4.0 keeps more of the attractive tail at some extra cost. Below about 2σ you cut into the well itself and the fluid stops condensing.

steps.title: The coefficients, and the ones you never write
steps.teach: Each pair of atom types needs its ε and σ. You will write two lines and get the third for free.

commands.explain: The Lennard-Jones coefficients for interactions between pairs of atoms that both have type 1: the energy parameter ε_{11} = 1.0 and the distance parameter σ_{11} = 1.0.

notes.note: ε, the depth of the potential well
notes.alternatives: A larger ε means a stronger attraction, and a fluid that condenses more readily.

notes.note: σ, the distance where the energy crosses zero
notes.alternatives: Roughly the diameter of the atom. There is no default for either value: lj/cut requires both.

commands.explain:
And for type 2 with type 2: ε_{22} = 0.5 and σ_{22} = 3.0 -- a shallower well but a much larger particle.

You never write a line for the 1-2 pair. By default LAMMPS mixes the unlike coefficients using geometric averages:

**ε_{ij} = √(ε_{ii} ε_{jj})**  and  **σ_{ij} = √(σ_{ii} σ_{jj})**

which here gives ε_{12} = √(1.0 × 0.5) = 0.707 and σ_{12} = √(1.0 × 3.0) = 1.732.

notes.note: ε for the heavy pair
notes.alternatives: Other mixing rules, including arithmetic averaging, can be selected with the pair_modify command.

steps.title: Ask for output
steps.teach: The system is now fully parameterised. Before running any dynamics, ask LAMMPS what to report.

commands.explain: Print thermodynamic information to the console every 10 simulation steps.

notes.note: steps between reports
notes.alternatives: Larger values print less and cost marginally less time. This run is short, so keep it frequent or you will see almost nothing.

commands.explain:
Choose the columns: the step number, the total energy E, and the pressure p.

These are *instantaneous* values of the named quantities at each output step, not cumulative averages. LAMMPS can also report data from compute styles, fix styles and variables, which is how running and sliding-window averages are done.

notes.note: the list of quantities to print
notes.alternatives: `temp`, `pe` and `ke` are the other common ones, and you will add them for the dynamics later. Whatever you list here is what the Charts window is able to plot.

steps.title: Compute the energy once, without moving anything
steps.teach: `run 0` is the cheapest possible check that a system is complete and self-consistent: it initialises forces and energies without advancing time at all.

commands.explain: Initialise forces and energy without actually running the simulation.

notes.note: number of timesteps to take -- none
notes.alternatives: Any positive number runs that many steps of dynamics, but only once something is integrating the equations of motion. Nothing is yet, so this would do nothing anyway.

notes.note: suppress the post-run summary
notes.alternatives: Leaving `post no` out prints the usual timing and statistics block, which is noise for a zero-step run.

steps.title: Run it
steps.teach:
Your system is complete: a box, 1600 atoms, masses, and interactions. Run it once and let LAMMPS confirm that.

The run should finish immediately. With the default settings the GUI opens two windows: the Output window with the console text, and a Charts window -- which will be empty, because no simulation steps were performed.
steps.expect: no error, and a single line of output at step 0

steps.title: The first number, and why it is positive
steps.teach:
The Output window shows the total energy and pressure at step 0, as the thermodynamic data request asked. The columns are headed `TotEng` and `Press`: LAMMPS prints its own names for these quantities rather than echoing the `etotal` and `press` keywords you wrote.

The total energy is large and **positive**. That is expected, and it is the reason the next act exists. The atoms were placed at random, and `overlap 0.3` prevented only the very worst contacts -- 0.3 is still well inside σ for the heavy species. Plenty of pairs therefore sit on the steep repulsive branch of the potential, the r^{−12} term in the equation above, where the energy is enormous.
steps.call_to_action: Look at the TotEng column in the Output window.

steps.title: Relax the structure
steps.teach:
Rather than start dynamics from a bad configuration, first let the atoms slide downhill into a nearby minimum of the potential energy.

LAMMPS computes the forces on all atoms and updates their positions using those forces, aiming to reduce the potential energy. The default algorithm is conjugate gradient. It stops as soon as **any one** of four criteria is met, and reports which one it was.

Except for trivial systems, a minimizer finds a *local* minimum, never the global one.

commands.explain: This takes the place of the `run 0 post no` line, which has done its job. It performs an iterative energy minimization.

notes.note: energy tolerance, then force tolerance, then the maximum number of iterations and of force evaluations
notes.alternatives: Tightening the tolerances makes the minimization work harder before it stops; raising the two limits lets it run longer before giving up. Whichever criterion is met first ends it.

steps.title: Watch the energy fall
steps.teach:
The GUI captures the output and updates the chart in real time as the minimization proceeds.

This run finishes quickly, so the GUI may miss some of the thermodynamic data. If that happens, reduce the data update interval in Preferences and switch to single-threaded, unaccelerated execution in the Accelerators tab. Each new attempt starts fresh and re-executes the script from the beginning.
steps.expect: the potential energy dropping quickly, then more gradually, then levelling off

steps.title: Positive to negative
steps.teach:
The potential energy U decreases from a positive value to a negative one, first rapidly and then more gradually before plateauing. That sign change is the whole story: the atoms have moved from being jammed against each other to sitting at reasonable distances, near the bottom of the potential well.

During minimization nothing is moving -- atoms are relocated, not given velocities -- so the kinetic energy K is zero throughout and the total energy is simply the potential energy, E = U.
steps.call_to_action: Look at the energy curve in the Charts window.
steps.expect: energy crossing from positive to negative and flattening out

steps.title: See your system
steps.teach:
The snapshot button sits in the status bar, two along from Run. Press it to render the current state and compare it with the system before minimization. The atoms are visibly clumping together as they move towards positions of lower potential energy.

The image viewer works by asking LAMMPS to render the current system with its own `dump image` machinery, so this is your system, not an illustration of one.
steps.call_to_action: Press the snapshot button, two along from Run.
steps.expect: atoms gathered into contact rather than scattered at random

steps.title: Watch more quantities
steps.teach:
After the minimization the overlapping atoms have been displaced and the system is ready for molecular dynamics. Since LAMMPS reads the script top to bottom, these lines simply follow the `minimize` command -- there is no need to re-initialise or redefine the system.

Once the atoms move there is a non-zero temperature T, and therefore a non-zero kinetic energy K, worth monitoring. The potential energy is U, and the three are related by **U + K = E**.

commands.explain: Report less often now: this run is far longer than the minimization was. The command is the same one you used in Part A, with 50 in place of 10.

commands.text: thermo_style custom step temp etotal pe ke press
commands.explain: Add temperature, potential energy and kinetic energy to the columns. You can check U + K = E directly, column by column, in the output.

steps.title: Integrate the equations of motion
steps.teach:
Nothing moves in LAMMPS unless a *fix* makes it move.

Since the only command affecting forces and velocities in this script is `fix nve`, and periodic boundaries apply in all directions, the simulation runs in the microcanonical (NVE) ensemble: constant number of particles, constant volume, constant energy. The system exchanges energy with nothing outside the box.

commands.explain: Update the positions and velocities of every atom in the group `all` at every step, integrating Newton's equations of motion with the velocity-Verlet algorithm.

notes.note: an ID you choose, used later to modify or remove this fix
the group of atoms it acts on
notes.alternatives: `all` is a default group containing every atom. Defining your own groups lets you integrate or thermostat only part of a system.

notes.note: the fix style
notes.alternatives: `nvt` adds a thermostat and holds temperature rather than energy; `npt` also controls pressure by letting the box change size.

commands.explain: Advance time in steps of 0.005 reduced time units.

notes.note: how far time moves in one step
notes.alternatives: Raise this too far and the integrator steps an atom straight through its neighbour's repulsive core. You will do exactly that on purpose shortly.

commands.explain: 25000 steps at 0.005 each is 125 reduced time units of dynamics.

steps.title: Run the dynamics
steps.teach: The system starts far from equilibrium. The minimized structure has no thermal motion at all, so the atoms accelerate down the potential gradients: the potential energy falls while the kinetic energy climbs.
steps.expect: potential energy falling while kinetic energy rises, both eventually levelling off

steps.title: Nobody chose that temperature
steps.teach:
After a few tens of thousands of steps both energies plateau and the total fluctuates around a constant value. That fluctuation, rather than a steady climb, is what a healthy NVE run looks like.

The temperature starts at zero and rises to a plateau of roughly 1.5. Nobody chose that number: it is whatever the potential energy released during equilibration happens to produce. Choosing the temperature is what a thermostat is for, and that comes next.
steps.call_to_action: Switch the Charts window between TotEng, PotEng and KinEng.
steps.expect: a flat TotEng with PotEng and KinEng trading against each other

steps.title: Choose the temperature instead of accepting it
steps.teach:
A Langevin thermostat subjects the atoms to friction and to random noise, in the form of randomly added velocities. Because a constant friction term removes more kinetic energy from fast atoms and less from slow ones, the system reaches a dynamic equilibrium where the energy removed and added are about equal.

With a thermostat present the simulation is no longer microcanonical: it samples the canonical (NVT) ensemble.

commands.explain: Add a Langevin thermostat to every atom, holding the temperature at 1.0 throughout the run.

notes.note: the target temperature at the start of the run, then at the end
notes.alternatives: The two numbers are the target at the beginning and at the end. Making them differ ramps the temperature over the run, which is how you heat or quench a system.

notes.note: the damping parameter
notes.alternatives: It determines how rapidly the temperature is relaxed towards its target. Smaller values couple more strongly and disturb the dynamics more; larger values equilibrate more slowly.

notes.note: the seed for the random forces
notes.alternatives: Change it to perform statistically independent simulations of the same system.

steps.title: A second script
steps.teach:
That script builds a system and equilibrates it, but it rebuilds everything from scratch every time it runs, and it mixes the two species from the start.

The rest of this tutorial performs more advanced operations: controlling where the atoms start, and restarting a simulation from a saved configuration. It works on two further files that came with the download. The first, now open, holds Part A without any commands in the System definition section.
steps.call_to_action: Read the sections that are already filled in.

steps.title: Place the two species apart
steps.teach: Create the atoms of types 1 and 2 in two separate regions: type 2 inside a cylinder, type 1 outside it. Watching them mix afterwards is far more informative than watching an already-mixed system stay mixed.

commands.explain: The same box as before.
And the same two atom types.

commands.text: region cyl_in cylinder z 0 0 10 INF INF side in
commands.explain: Two regions representing the inside and the outside of a cylinder of radius 10, running the full height of the box along z.

notes.note: the cylinder axis
notes.alternatives: `x` or `y` orient it differently. The two INF values run it the full length of the box in that direction.

notes.note: which side of the surface counts as the region
notes.alternatives: `side in` is the inside; `side out` is everything in the box that is not the cylinder. The next line is exactly that complement.

commands.text: region cyl_out cylinder z 0 0 10 INF INF side out
commands.explain: The complement of the same cylinder.
1000 light atoms placed only outside the cylinder, and 150 heavy atoms only inside it. The regions replace `simbox` as the placement volume.
The heavy species, confined to the cylinder.

steps.title: Save the result
steps.teach: Add a sixth section at the end of the file, after the `minimize` command. This is the key improvement: writing the state to a file means the next script can start from it, rather than repeating the system creation and the minimization.

commands.explain: Write the state of the system to a text file. It contains everything needed to restart: the number of atoms, the box size, the masses, the pair coefficients, and the final positions with their IDs and types. The last three columns of the Atoms section are image flags recording which atoms crossed a periodic boundary.

notes.note: the file to write
notes.alternatives: `write_restart` writes a binary file instead: more compact, faster to write, and it records the atom and pair styles too, so those commands need not be reissued. But restart files are not portable between LAMMPS versions or platforms, which is why the tutorials use a data file.

steps.title: Build it and save it
steps.teach:
This run creates the file the next script reads. You can inspect it afterwards by right-clicking the file name in the editor and choosing to view it.

The tour waits here rather than moving on by itself: the next step opens a different script, and the charts from this run are worth a look first.

steps.title: The third script
steps.teach:
This file holds only the Initialization section; everything else comes from the data file you just wrote.

One ordering catch: because most of the information is read from the file, the System definition and Settings sections are not repeated -- but `pair_style` is the exception. It must now come **before** the simulation box is defined, and therefore before `read_data`.

steps.title: Read the saved system
steps.teach:
Two lines replace the whole System definition and Settings sections of the first script.

These are both new to you, so they are written out for you as usual. Read them before you accept them: `read_data` is the command that will start most of your own scripts from now on, and the order of these two lines is the point of this step.
steps.call_to_action: Read both lines, then press Tab to accept them.

commands.explain: The pair style must be set before the box exists. The data file carries the coefficients but not the style itself, so write the same `lj/cut` style with the same 4.0 cutoff you used in Part A.
Rebuild the box, the atoms, the masses and the pair coefficients from the file written by the previous script.

steps.title: Clean up the misplaced atoms
steps.teach:
Visualising the system shows that some atoms left their original region during the minimization. To start from a clean slate -- only type 2 inside the cylinder and only type 1 outside it -- delete the misplaced ones.

The regions have to be defined again first: regions are not saved by `write_data`.

commands.text: region cyl_in cylinder z 0 0 10 INF INF side in
commands.explain: Recreate the two regions, since a data file does not store them.

commands.text: region cyl_out cylinder z 0 0 10 INF INF side out
commands.explain: And the complement.
Two groups containing all atoms of type 1 and all atoms of type 2 respectively.

notes.note: how the group is built
notes.alternatives: `region` selects by position, `id` by atom number, and `union`, `intersect` and `subtract` combine existing groups. That composability is the point.

commands.explain: The heavy species.
Two more groups built from position rather than type: the atoms inside and outside the cylinder.

notes.note: membership is evaluated now, not continuously
notes.alternatives: These groups are created based on the atoms' positions at the moment the command is read. The group keeps those atoms even after they move, which is what makes the deletion below well defined.

commands.explain: And those outside it.
The intersections: light atoms that ended up inside the cylinder, and heavy atoms that ended up outside it. These are the ones that do not belong.
The heavy atoms on the wrong side.

Delete both misplaced sets, leaving a clean starting arrangement.

LAMMPS allows a limited number of custom groups (30), so it is good practice to delete groups that are no longer needed with `group <name> delete`.
And the same on the other side.

steps.title: Measure the mixing
steps.teach:
Now the interesting part: measure how the two species mix rather than only watching them.

Two equal-style variables count how many atoms of each type are inside the cylinder as a function of time. Then two computes measure the coordination number -- how many type 2 atoms sit near each type 1 atom, within a cutoff -- and average it. That average is a good indicator of the degree of mixing in a binary mixture.

commands.explain: Count the atoms of a given group that are currently within a given region. Equal-style variables are expressions evaluated during the run that return a number.

notes.note: the variable style
notes.alternatives: Other LAMMPS variable styles include `atom`, `index`, `file`, `loop`, `string` and `vector`. Only `equal` returns a single number suitable for a thermo column.

commands.explain: The same count for the heavy species.

commands.text: compute coor12 grp_t1 coord/atom cutoff 2 group grp_t2
commands.explain: For each atom of type 1, count how many type 2 atoms lie within 2 length units. The `/atom` suffix means this produces one value per atom rather than a single number.

notes.note: the compute style
notes.alternatives: The suffix tells you what a compute produces: no suffix is global data, `/atom` per-atom, `/local` local, `/chunk` per-chunk, `/grid` per-grid. A per-atom quantity has to be reduced before it can be printed.

commands.text: compute sumcoor12 grp_t1 reduce ave c_coor12
commands.explain:
Average that per-atom coordination number over all type 1 atoms, giving one number per step.

Computes neither print anything nor run by themselves: they need a consumer that references them. Here the first compute is referenced by the second, and the second is referenced by the thermo_style command below.

notes.note: referencing another compute
notes.alternatives: The `c_` prefix means the output of compute coor12. Without a consumer, the first compute would never be evaluated at all.

steps.title: Print the measurements, and run
steps.teach: Add the two variables and the averaged coordination to the information printed during the simulation, give the atoms an initial temperature, and thermostat them.

commands.text: thermo_style custom step temp etotal v_n1_in v_n2_in c_sumcoor12
commands.explain: A `custom` style listing, in order: `step`, `temp`, `etotal`, then your two variables and your compute. The `v_` prefix pulls in a variable and the `c_` prefix a compute, so `n1_in` becomes `v_n1_in` and `sumcoor12` becomes `c_sumcoor12`. That is what puts your own measurements alongside the standard quantities.

steps.title: Set it moving
steps.teach: The last section: give the atoms velocities, integrate them, and hold the temperature.

commands.text: velocity all create 1.0 49284 mom yes dist gaussian
commands.explain: Give every atom a velocity drawn from a Gaussian distribution corresponding to a temperature of 1.0, with zero net momentum for the system as a whole.

notes.note: remove the net momentum of the system
notes.alternatives: Without `mom yes` the whole system can drift bodily through the box. That drift contributes to the measured temperature without representing any thermal motion.

notes.note: the shape of the velocity distribution
notes.alternatives: `gaussian` matches what an equilibrated system actually looks like; `uniform` is the alternative and equilibrates to the same place, just less directly.

commands.explain: Integrate the motion, as before.

commands.text: fix mylgv all langevin 1.0 1.0 0.1 10917 zero yes
commands.explain: Thermostat at a constant temperature of 1.0. `zero yes` keeps the random thermostat forces from introducing a net momentum of their own.
The same stable timestep you used in Part A: 0.005 reduced time units.
Long enough for the two species to genuinely interdiffuse.

steps.title: Watch them mix
steps.teach: This is the longest run in the tutorial. You are now measuring something, not just simulating it.
steps.expect: n1_in rising and n2_in falling as the two species interdiffuse

steps.title: The measurement, not the picture
steps.teach:
`n1_in` climbs as light atoms wander into the cylinder and `n2_in` falls as heavy ones leave it. The averaged coordination number rises towards a plateau, and that plateau is the mixed state.

This is the difference between watching a simulation and doing science with one. The snapshot is suggestive; the curve is evidence.
steps.call_to_action: Select each column in turn in the Charts window.
steps.expect: the coordination number rising and then flattening as mixing completes

steps.title: It is yours now
steps.teach:
Three things worth trying, each one number.

**Raise the timestep** to 0.05 and run again: the total energy climbs without bound, and the run may stop with **ERROR: Lost atoms**. The integrator has stepped an atom straight through its neighbour's repulsive core; it almost never means atoms were really lost, it means the integration went unstable.

**Deepen the heavy-atom well** with `pair_coeff 2 2 2.0 3.0` and see whether the species separate again instead of mixing.

**Ramp the temperature** by giving `fix langevin` different start and end values.

All the runs in these tutorials are deliberately kept short so they finish on a personal computer. None of them is long enough to produce statistically meaningful results.
steps.call_to_action: Change something and run it again.
